analysis.one_liner: Bars the consumer financial watchdog from examining small mortgage lenders unless other regulators request it.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had zero cosponsors, was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and died there without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) — the federal watchdog for consumer financial products — from auditing, investigating, or suing "responsible community mortgage lenders" unless another regulator specifically asked it to. To qualify, a lender would have to be small (under $2 billion in assets for banks and credit unions, or under $50 million in net worth for independent lenders, and under 25,000 loans or $5 billion in annual volume) with a mostly clean two-year record. It also would have limited the government's ability to require these lenders to audit their outside contractors, and adjusted how 2016 loan volume is counted for a lending-rule threshold.
analysis.who_benefits: Small community mortgage lenders — community banks, credit unions, and independent nonbank lenders that meet the bill's size and clean-record tests. They would no longer face CFPB examinations or enforcement actions on their own initiative, and would only have to audit their vendors and contractors if a regulator already had reason to suspect a violation. This would cut their compliance and legal costs and reduce their exposure to federal penalties. The bill's own text argues this relief would keep small lenders in the market and preserve consumer choice among local lenders.

how_it_helps.text: Lenders meeting the size limits (under $2 billion in assets for banks and credit unions, or $50 million in net worth for independent lenders, and under 25,000 loans or $5 billion in annual volume) and with no court finding or cease-and-desist order tied to their mortgage lending in the prior two years would be off-limits to CFPB audits, examinations, investigations, and enforcement unless a state regulator, a federal loan-guarantee agency, the housing finance regulator, or another supervisor requested it.

The CFPB and federal banking agencies could only require a qualifying lender to audit a vendor or third-party contractor if the regulator already had reasonable cause to believe the contractor was causing the lender to break the law, rather than as routine oversight.

For calendar year 2016, the bill would count a lender's loan originations using only the preceding two years instead of three when measuring against the qualified-mortgage threshold, making it easier for newer or growing lenders to reach the 95% qualified-mortgage share needed for the exemptions.

analysis.who_pays: The CFPB would lose its ability to independently detect and stop problems at these lenders — it could only act if another agency asked. Borrowers who get mortgages from community banks, credit unions, and small nonbank lenders would be relying on state and other federal regulators to spot abusive practices, since the federal consumer watchdog could not look on its own. The bill's supporters argue other regulators and market oversight would fill the gap.

drawbacks.text: The CFPB could no longer independently examine or take enforcement action against a qualifying lender even if it saw a pattern of problems; it could act only when a state regulator, a federal loan-guarantee agency, the housing finance regulator, or another supervisor requested it, which narrows the federal safety net for borrowers using small and nonbank lenders.

The vendor-audit relief means a lender would not have to scrutinize the outside contractors that often handle servicing, collections, and foreclosure work unless a regulator already suspected a violation — removing a routine check on a channel where mortgage abuses have historically surfaced.

The 'responsible' label only looks back two years and only disqualifies lenders with a court finding or a cease-and-desist order, so lenders subject to other forms of discipline or recent settlements short of those markers would still qualify for the exemption.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real: examinations and enforcement defense are costly for small lenders, and the bill's narrow size and clean-record tests would exclude larger or recently sanctioned firms. But the trade is straightforward — the compliance savings for these lenders come directly out of independent federal oversight of the mortgages their customers take out, and the CFPB's ability to act would depend entirely on other regulators asking it to. Since small and nonbank lenders are where many consumers actually get mortgages, the reduction in oversight is the price of the relief, and the bill offered no replacement mechanism for catching problems.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Roger Williams introduced the bill on July 14, 2016, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The CFPB kept its full authority to examine and sue small mortgage lenders on its own initiative, and borrowers kept the independent federal watchdog that this bill would have fenced off. Small mortgage lenders, who would have gained the exam and enforcement exemptions, are the ones who lost out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The CFPB and the borrowers it protects

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Standing committee with jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Jeb Hensarling (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the referral — no hearing, no markup, and no vote was ever scheduled, so the bill died in committee at the end of the 114th Congress.

against.name: House members of both parties
against.what_they_did: None of the other 434 House members cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no demonstrated support beyond its sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only support on the record was a single Republican sponsor, with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.industry: Small community mortgage lenders (community banks, credit unions, and small nonbank lenders)
industries.note: The bill would have exempted qualifying lenders from CFPB examinations, investigations, and enforcement, and from routine vendor-audit requirements, cutting their compliance costs and legal exposure. The relief comes directly out of the independent federal oversight that protects the borrowers who take out these lenders' mortgages.

The bill's stated aim was to keep small lenders competitive and prevent consolidation, which would have marginally limited large lenders' market share. At the same time, CFPB scrutiny would have remained focused on larger lenders, who get no relief under the bill.
